lead: A PWM AC voltage controller, or AC chopper, switches the load between the 50 Hz supply and a short circuit many thousand times a second. The fraction of each switching period spent on the supply, the duty ratio D, sets the output. Because every switching period passes a slice of the supply, the 50 Hz part of the output stays in phase with the supply and the unwanted frequencies sit near the switching frequency, where a small LC filter removes them.
prereq: You need: phase control and its harmonics from AC voltage controllers: phase and on-off control, and IGBT and MOSFET switching from power semiconductor devices.

blocks.text: The power stage has two switches. S1, the series switch, joins the supply to the load; S2, the freewheeling switch, sits across the load. Both must be bidirectional, because voltage and current reverse every half cycle: each is two IGBTs joined emitter to emitter, each with its antiparallel diode. A TRIAC is far too slow for kilohertz switching.

items: S1 on, S2 off: the load sees the supply voltage v<sub>s</sub>.
S1 off, S2 on: the load is shorted, its voltage is zero, and an inductive load current keeps flowing through S2.
They must never be on together (a supply short) nor, with an inductive load, both fully off (an open load), so each changeover follows the sign of the supply voltage.

blocks.text: The switching frequency f<sub>sw</sub> is typically 5 kHz to 20 kHz for IGBTs. The load is connected for t<sub>on</sub> = DT of each period T and shorted for the rest.

sections.h3: Duty ratio, RMS value and harmonics

blocks.text: D = tₒₙ/T,   Vₒ = Vₛ √D,   V₁ = D·Vₛ
blocks.where: V<sub>o</sub> is the RMS of the chopped load voltage and V<sub>1</sub> the RMS of its 50 Hz part, with V<sub>s</sub> the RMS supply voltage.

blocks.text: The squared output is v<sub>s</sub>² for a fraction D of the time, which gives V<sub>s</sub>√D. The output is v<sub>s</sub>(t) times a switching function that is 1 for a fraction D of each period: its average D gives the 50 Hz part D·v<sub>s</sub>, and its terms at f<sub>sw</sub>, 2f<sub>sw</sub>, … give sidebands at m·f<sub>sw</sub> ± f. The lowest is f<sub>sw</sub> − f: 9950 Hz for a 10 kHz chopper on 50 Hz.

V<sub>o</sub> exceeds V<sub>1</sub> by the sideband content. A heater uses that power, but a motor would only be heated by it, so other loads get an output LC filter and then see close to D·v<sub>s</sub>.

With a resistor and no filter, the supply current is a pulse train of RMS V<sub>s</sub>√D/R while the power is D·V<sub>s</sub>²/R, so the power factor is √D. An LC input filter with its corner well between 50 Hz and f<sub>sw</sub> supplies the pulses from its capacitor, and the supply delivers only their 50 Hz average, D·v<sub>s</sub>/R, in phase with v<sub>s</sub>. The power factor then rises close to 1.
Raising f<sub>sw</sub> lets the filter L and C shrink roughly as 1/f<sub>sw</sub>, but switching loss rises roughly in proportion to f<sub>sw</sub>. Below about 20 kHz the inductor can whine audibly.

Uses: AC voltage stabilisers, electronic tap changers and motor soft starting with a good input power factor. A three-phase chopper has a series switch in each line and three freewheeling switches joined in star across the load, shorting all three load terminals together during the off-time. Some syllabi call it an AC chopper.

examples.question: A 230 V, 50 Hz supply feeds a 50 Ω resistor through a single-phase PWM AC chopper switching at 10 kHz with D = 0.6 and no output filter. Find t<sub>on</sub>, V<sub>o</sub>, the power, V<sub>1</sub> and its share of the power, the lowest sideband, and the supply power factor without and with an ideal input filter.
steps: V<sub>1</sub> = 0.6 × 230 = 138.0 V. Its power is 138.0²/50 = 380.9 W; the other 253.9 W is carried by the sidebands.
Lowest unwanted frequency: f<sub>sw</sub> − f = 10 000 − 50 = 9950 Hz, the 199th harmonic of 50 Hz.
Ideal filter: the supply gives only the 50 Hz average, 138.0/50 = 2.76 A, in phase. Check: 230 × 2.76 = 634.8 W. PF = 1.
examples.answer: t<sub>on</sub> = 60 µs, V<sub>o</sub> = 178.2 V, P = 634.8 W, V<sub>1</sub> = 138.0 V carrying 380.9 W, lowest sideband 9950 Hz, power factor 0.775 without a filter and close to 1 with one.

examples.question: For the chopper above, design the input LC filter with C = 10 µF and a corner frequency of 1 kHz. Find L, the attenuation at 9950 Hz, and the power factor once the capacitor's own 50 Hz current is included.
steps: Far above the corner an LC filter attenuates by about (f/f<sub>c</sub>)² = (9950/1000)² = 99, so only about 1 % of the 9950 Hz current reaches the supply.
The capacitor draws 230/X<sub>C</sub> with X<sub>C</sub> = 1/(2π × 50 × 10 × 10⁻⁶) = 318.3 Ω: 0.72 A, leading by 90°.
Supply current = √(2.76² + 0.72²) = 2.85 A. Power factor = 2.76/2.85 = 0.97, leading.
examples.answer: L = 2.53 mH; the 9950 Hz sideband is cut about 99 times; the supply power factor is about 0.97 leading, against 0.775 without the filter.

traps: Calling D·V<sub>s</sub> the RMS output. It is the 50 Hz part; the RMS of the chopped wave is V<sub>s</sub>√D, which is larger: 178.2 V against 138.0 V at D = 0.6.
Claiming the unfiltered supply current is sinusoidal. It is a pulse train with power factor √D; only the input filter makes the supply see a sine.
Using one IGBT with an antiparallel diode as the AC switch. It blocks only one polarity; two devices back to back are needed.
Writing that a plain dead time is safe with an inductive load. With both switches off, the load current has no path; the changeover must follow the voltage or current sign.

quiz.q: Give the RMS output and the 50 Hz part of the output of an ideal PWM AC chopper with a resistive load.
quiz.a: V<sub>o</sub> = V<sub>s</sub>√D and V<sub>1</sub> = D·V<sub>s</sub>, with D = t<sub>on</sub>/T.

quiz.q: Why must both switches of the chopper be bidirectional?
quiz.a: Voltage and current reverse every half cycle, so each switch must block both polarities and conduct both ways: two IGBTs back to back.

quiz.q: Why does the unfiltered supply current give a power factor of only √D, even with a resistor?
quiz.a: The current is the load current switched on for a fraction D of each period, so its RMS is V<sub>s</sub>√D/R while the power is D·V<sub>s</sub>²/R. PF = D V<sub>s</sub>²/R ÷ (V<sub>s</sub> × V<sub>s</sub>√D/R) = √D.

quiz.q: A 230 V supply feeds a 20 Ω resistor through an AC chopper with D = 0.4. Find V<sub>o</sub>, V<sub>1</sub> and the load power.
At what frequency is the lowest sideband of a 20 kHz chopper on a 50 Hz supply?
At half power into a resistor, compare the input power factor of a phase controller and a filtered PWM chopper, and explain the difference.
quiz.a: Phase control at α = 90° gives 0.707: the chopped current has a 3rd harmonic of over half the fundamental, and its 50 Hz part lags by about 32°. The filtered chopper draws only the in-phase 50 Hz average current, so its power factor is close to 1 (0.97 with the filter of worked example 2).

quiz.q: What happens when f<sub>sw</sub> is raised from 5 kHz to 40 kHz?
quiz.a: L and C can each be about one eighth as large and the whine moves above hearing, but switching loss rises about eight times, so efficiency drops and the heat sink grows.

beyond: Not for the exam. SiC and GaN switches push AC choppers to tens of kilohertz with small filters, which is what makes solid-state transformers and fast voltage restorers practical. Repeat the bidirectional switch cell nine times and you reach the matrix converter. Search for "AC chopper commutation", "PWM AC voltage regulator" and "dynamic voltage restorer".

figure.caption: One supply cycle of the chopper of the worked example with D = 0.6. Each period passes 0.6 of the supply wave and shorts the load for the rest; the 50 Hz part of the output is 0.6 times the supply.

spec.aria: Chopped load voltage pulses under a 50 hertz sine, with the smooth 0.6 times supply curve drawn through them.
